transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's just this exhaustion. I mean, I don't know if exhaustion is even the right word for it anymore. It's more like this heavy, pulling weight that just drags me down all day, every day. What brought me in is I’m so worn out that even walking from the bedroom to the kitchen feels like hauling lumber all day. And I know what hauling lumber feels like, I used to do some construction work back in my twenties when I was taking a few college classes, and let me tell you, this is worse. At least then, you could sit down, have a cold drink, get a good night's sleep, and wake up feeling ready to go again. But this? Resting doesn’t give me anything back. I can lie in bed for twelve, fourteen hours, just staring at the ceiling, or maybe dozing off and on, but when I finally force myself to swing my legs over the edge of the mattress, it's like I haven't slept in a week. My bones ache with it, my muscles just feel like lead. It takes me twenty minutes just to convince myself to stand up, and by the time I make it to the kitchen to pour a glass of water, I'm ready to collapse again. It's just... it's completely draining the life out of me, and I don't know how much longer I can keep trying to push through it when there's nothing left in the tank to push with.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, let me think... if I trace it back, really trace it back to when this specific kind of heavy feeling started, I'd have to say it's been about four months. Yeah, four months, almost exactly. It was right around the time my wife went back to working full-time. She had been home a lot more before that, and, well, we had a rhythm, you know? A routine. But she had to take this full-time position, and suddenly her schedule changed completely. 

So for the last four months, she's gone from early in the morning until the evening, and I started spending most weekdays entirely alone in the house. And let me tell you, when you're used to having someone around, even just hearing them moving around in the other room or making coffee, the silence of an empty house is... it's a lot. It changes things. I thought I'd be fine, I thought I'd use the time to get things done around the place, maybe tackle some projects I've been putting off in the garage. But almost the exact week she started that full-time shift and I was left here by myself Monday through Friday, that's when this drain really pulled the plug on me. The days just stretch out forever when you're alone like that, and you start noticing every little creak of the floorboards, and the energy just seeps right out of you. So, yes, four months of this. Four months of just me and the empty house.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before this heavy feeling started?

No. No, I really don't. And that's... that's maybe the hardest part to explain to people, because they think you're just being lazy or antisocial, but it's not that. It's like the color has just been drained out of everything. 

Take the choir, for instance. I've been singing bass in our church choir for, gosh, probably fifteen years. Every Wednesday night practice, every Sunday morning service. I used to love it, the harmony, the fellowship, just being part of something bigger. But now? The thought of getting dressed, driving over there, standing up for an hour, and trying to smile at everyone... I just can't. I haven't been in two months. The director, Dave, he's a good guy, he texts me asking where I am, if I'm sick, and I don't even reply. I just look at the phone and I can't even summon the energy to type back "I'm not coming." 

And it's not just that. I used to play pickup basketball at the Y on Saturday mornings. Nothing serious, just a bunch of older guys trying not to pull a hamstring, you know? It was a great way to sweat and joke around. I haven't laced up my sneakers since this whole thing started. Same with working on cars. I’ve got this '68 Mustang in the garage, a project I’ve been tinkering with forever. I used to spend whole weekends out there, getting grease under my fingernails, listening to the radio. Now, I walk past the garage door and I don't even want to look at it. It just feels like a giant pile of metal that demands things from me. 

Even... even just grilling for the family. We used to do burgers and dogs every Sunday afternoon if the weather was decent. The kids would come over, maybe some neighbors. I loved being the guy at the grill, flipping burgers, handing out beers. Now, my wife suggests it and I just feel this pit in my stomach. The idea of buying the meat, cleaning the grates, standing out there... it's just too much. I can't make myself care. I can't make myself care about any of it anymore, doctor. It's all just... empty.
Have you been having any thoughts about death, or wishing you weren't alive, since this heavy feeling started?

Well... I mean, yes. Yes, I have. It's... it's hard to say out loud, because you know how people react when you bring up things like this, but... the thought just keeps coming that I should just be dead. It just keeps coming back, over and over. It’s like a broken record playing in the back of my mind all day long. Just this heavy, constant drumbeat of, 'You should be dead. It would be so much easier if you were just dead.' 

And it's not just a passing thought, doctor, it just sits right there in the room with me. Especially with my wife working those long hours now, like I was telling you before. I'm just here, by myself, wandering from the bedroom to the living room or just sitting in the recliner for six, seven hours straight. And that's the part that really gets to me, because when I’m alone... it scares me. It genuinely terrifies me. Because the house is so quiet, and that thought gets so loud, and I start thinking I might actually do something to make that happen. 

I’ll be sitting there, staring at the carpet, and suddenly my mind is just racing, thinking about how I could do it, what I would use. I start thinking about the garage, the heavy extension cords, the things I used to use for my car projects, and they don't look like tools or supplies anymore, you know? They look like a way out of this exhaustion. And I have to force myself to stay inside the house, to lock the door to the garage so I don't go out there, but even then, I'm just pacing the hallway, completely terrified of my own brain. Because what if one of these long, empty afternoons I don't stop myself? I just can't shake this fear that I'm actually going to do something to make it happen before she even gets home from work. It's just... it's a terrifying place to be in your own head.
Have you experienced any strange sensations, heard voices, or seen things that aren't there since this heavy feeling started?

Well... I didn't know if I should mention this, because it's... it's the kind of thing that makes people look at you differently, but yes. Yes, I have. And it goes right back to what I was saying before, about the house being so incredibly quiet when my wife is at her full-time job. When she's at work and it's just me, the silence gets so heavy, but then... then it's not silent anymore. 

I hear voices. And I don't mean like a vague whispering in my head or my own thoughts, I mean it is as clear as somebody physically standing right there in the hallway just outside the living room. The first time it happened, I actually got out of my chair and walked out there because I swore someone had gotten into the house. I checked the front door, I checked the locks, but there was nobody. Just me. But the voices, they... they say terrible things. They sound like they're just standing out there in the hall and they tell me that I'm a burden. They just keep saying it, that I'm a massive burden to my wife, to my kids, to everybody. They tell me that my family would be so much better off without me. 

And it's just so real, doctor, it echoes off the walls just like a real person speaking, telling me how useless I am and how they'd all be relieved if I was just gone. It's not muffled, it's not distant, it's right there in the house with me. And I can't make it stop. I just have to sit there in the empty house, terrified, listening to somebody who isn't there tell me how much better my family's life would be if I wasn't around to ruin it.
Do the voices you hear tell you to do anything specific, or are they just critical of you?

Well... no, they don't... they don't give me orders, if that's what you mean. They aren't saying, you know, 'go out to the garage and do this' or 'go grab that.' It's not like a set of instructions. It's really just... just what I was saying a minute ago. It's this relentless criticism that just beats me down until there's nothing left. 

Like I mentioned, it always seems to happen when my wife is at work. She's picking up all these extra hours now to keep us afloat because I'm just... well, I'm not doing anything. And when she's gone, the house gets so terribly quiet. You can hear the refrigerator hum, you can hear the clock ticking in the kitchen, and it's just this heavy, suffocating silence. And then... then out of nowhere, clear as somebody standing right there in the hallway, the voice just starts. 

It just hammers away at me, telling me I'm a burden. Just a massive, useless weight on everyone. It doesn't tell me exactly what to do, it just tells me that my family would be so much better off without me. It goes on about how my wife wouldn't have to work so hard, how the kids wouldn't have to be ashamed of a dad who can't even get out of a recliner. It just repeats it, over and over, echoing out there in the hall, sounding so real I still catch myself looking over my shoulder to see who's there. So, no, not specific commands... just tearing me apart, making sure I know exactly how much easier everyone's life would be if I just wasn't around anymore.
Do the voices you hear only appear when you are feeling your worst emotionally, or can they occur at any time?

Well... that's a good question, doctor, and I've thought about that a lot. I really have. Because when you start hearing things, you start trying to figure out why, you know? You try to trace it back. And... well, the truth is, I never, ever heard voices back when I was myself. Never. I mean, before all this started, I was a pretty normal guy. I went to work, I came home, I worked on my car projects out in the garage, I spent time with my wife and kids. I was just... normal. I never had anything like this happen. I never heard people talking in the hallway, I never thought I was being punished for anything, none of that. 

It wasn't until... well, until I just sank down into this hole. This awful, heavy depression where I just couldn't do anything anymore. I stopped going to work, I stopped going out to the garage, I stopped even getting dressed most days. I just stopped keeping up with my life entirely. And it was only after that happened, after I was already just drowning in this feeling of being completely worthless and stuck in that recliner for hours on end, that the voices started. It's like... it's like the worse I feel, the louder they get. When the house is quiet and I'm just sitting there, feeling like I can't even lift my arms because I'm so exhausted and so sad, that's when they show up. They didn't exist before this dark cloud settled over me. It's only now, when I'm at my absolute lowest, when I'm just a shell of who I used to be, that they come around to tell me how awful I am. So, yes, it's definitely tied to this... this state I'm in now. Never before. Only since I lost myself.
How long have you been having these thoughts about wanting to be dead?

Well... I suppose the thoughts really started creeping in around the same time the heavy feeling took over everything. It wasn't an overnight thing, you know? It didn't just hit me all at once. It was more like... like a slow leak in a tire. At first, you just feel a little flat, a little tired. But then, as the weeks went by and I found myself just stuck in that recliner, unable to even muster the energy to go out to the garage and look at my tools... that's when the thoughts started. 

It began as just this vague idea, like, 'maybe it wouldn't be so bad if I just didn't wake up tomorrow.' Just a passing thought. But as I got worse, as I stopped going to work and my wife had to start picking up all those extra shifts, the thought just grew. It got louder, much like those voices in the hallway. And now... now it's just this constant, heavy presence. The thought keeps coming that I should just be dead. It’s like a drumbeat in the background of my mind, just repeating over and over that it would be the easiest solution for everyone.

And the thing is, doctor... it really scares me. It terrifies me, actually. Because it's one thing to have a passing thought, but it's another thing entirely when you're sitting in that silent house, listening to the refrigerator hum, and you realize you're actually entertaining the idea. When I’m alone, especially when my wife is at work and it's just me and that suffocating quiet... it scares me because I start thinking I might actually do something to make that happen. I start looking around the room, and my mind just goes to these dark, terrible places. I don't want to leave my family, I really don't, but when you're drowning and the voices are telling you you're a burden... sometimes you just want the water to finally take you under. So, it's been building for a while, but it's only recently that it's gotten to the point where I'm genuinely afraid of being left alone with my own mind.
Have you had any days or periods in the last four months where you felt significantly better than others?

Well... no. No, I really haven't. I wish I could sit here and tell you that I've had a good week, or even just a good couple of days where the fog lifted, but... it just hasn't happened. It's just been this one, long, continuous stretch of... of nothingness. And heaviness. 

I've tried to pinpoint exactly when it all started feeling this permanent, and it's been going on for about four months now. It really settled in right around the time my wife had to go back to working full-time. Before that, she was part-time, and she was around the house more, so there was at least some conversation, some movement in the house, you know? But then she took on all those extra hours to make up for my lack of income, and suddenly I was just... alone. 

For the last four months, I've just been spending most weekdays entirely by myself in that house. Monday through Friday, she leaves early, the kids go to school, and the door clicks shut, and then it's just me and that recliner. And that's when the silence really started to suffocate me. It's like the days just bleed into one another. You'd think maybe on a Tuesday the sun would shine differently or I'd wake up feeling a spark of energy to go look at the car in the garage, but... no. It's been four months of waking up, moving to the chair, listening to the refrigerator, hearing those awful voices in the hallway telling me I'm useless, and just waiting for the day to end. There hasn't been a single break in the clouds. Not one day where I felt like my old self again. It's just been four solid months of this heavy, dark weight pressing down on me, every single day, without fail.
Have there been any periods, no matter how brief, where your heavy feeling and thoughts of death significantly lessened or seemed to disappear since this all started four months ago?

Well... no, doctor. Not even for a little bit. I mean, I really wish I could say there was a morning where I woke up and the sun was shining and I thought, 'Hey, maybe today won't be so bad.' I wish I could tell you that maybe on a Sunday, when my wife is home and we're all together, that the weight lifts just a little, but... it doesn't. It really doesn't. 

Every single morning, it's the exact same thing. I wake up, and before I even open my eyes, I feel it. It's this... this incredibly heavy, hopeless feeling right here in my chest. It's like someone parked a truck on my ribs while I was sleeping. And it just stays there. It doesn't matter if it's Tuesday or Saturday, it doesn't matter if it's raining or sunny. It's just this constant, crushing weight. 

And you know, sometimes... sometimes I try to fight it. I really do. I'll force myself to get up out of that recliner, and I'll walk out to the garage. I'll look at my tools, look at the car I was working on before all this started. I'll tell myself, 'Just pick up a wrench. Just do one thing.' But... I can't. I just stand there. And then, before I even realize what's happening, I'm just sitting there on an old overturned bucket in the garage, and I'm crying. I'm just sitting there crying, and I don't even know what started it. I don't know why the tears are falling, I just know that the heaviness is so much that it's leaking out of me. It's just this overwhelming sadness that I can't shake, not even for a minute. So, no... there haven't been any breaks. Just this heavy, hopeless feeling, every single day.
Have you ever heard voices or experienced similar hallucinations when you weren't feeling depressed or overwhelmed?

No... no, never. I mean, back when I was myself, before all of this started... my mind was just, well, normal. I had regular thoughts, you know? Thinking about what tools I needed to pick up from the hardware store, or worrying about the electric bill, or just wondering what my wife was making for dinner. Just regular, everyday things. I never, ever heard voices whispering in the hallway back then. And I certainly never believed I was being punished for anything. I was just a normal guy living a normal life. I was working, I was keeping up with the house, I was doing exactly what I was supposed to do as a husband and a father. 

It was only after... well, after I really sank into this... this deep, dark hole, and I just completely stopped keeping up with my usual life. That's when it all changed. When I stopped going to work and started spending all day in that recliner, when I stopped paying the bills and my wife had to take on all that extra weight... that’s when the voices started creeping in. It’s like, once I stopped moving and stopped being useful, the silence in that house got so heavy that my brain just filled it with these awful things. 

It was only after I sank into this depression and stopped living my actual life that I started hearing them tell me how useless I am. That's when I started feeling like this whole thing, the heaviness and the voices, is some kind of punishment for me failing my family. Because I wasn't doing my part anymore, you see? But before this? Never. Not once. I never heard a single voice or thought I was being punished back when I was still me. It's like I'm a completely different person now, living in a completely different reality, and I just... I don't know how I got here from where I used to be. I really don't.
Have you had any episodes of depression like this before the current one that started four months ago?

No... no, I haven't. I mean, I'm 54 years old, and I've lived a whole lot of life before these last four months, and I can honestly tell you, I have never, ever felt anything even remotely close to this. 

I mean, sure, I've had bad days. Everyone has bad days, right? Like when the transmission blew on my old truck back in '08, or when they laid off a bunch of guys at my old job... I was stressed, sure. I worried about money, I lost a little sleep here and there. But I always bounced back. I always got up the next morning, drank my coffee, put my boots on, and went out to figure it out. I never just... stopped. 

This thing, this heavy, suffocating blanket that's on me now? It's completely new. It's like I woke up four months ago and somebody had completely rewired my brain while I was sleeping. I spent my whole life being the guy who fixes things, the guy who provides for his family, and I never had a single stretch of time where I couldn't get out of a chair or where I just sat in the garage and cried for no reason. So, no, doctor, nothing like this. Not ever. 

It's terrifying, honestly, because I don't have any experience with it. I don't know the rules. I keep looking back, trying to sift through my memories, trying to see if there were warning signs, you know? Maybe ten years ago, maybe twenty, maybe when the kids were little and things were tight... but there's just... nothing. I was just a regular, steady guy. I just don't understand how a man goes 54 years being one way, and then suddenly, he's just... broken. It just doesn't make any sense to me that this could happen out of nowhere.
Have you ever experienced an episode of depression similar to what you're going through now before the current one that started four months ago?

Well, like I was just saying... no, I haven't. I know you just asked me that, but the answer is still the same. I've been thinking and thinking about it, trying to figure out if maybe I missed something, you know? Like maybe there was a time in my thirties or forties where I felt a little down, but... no. Nothing like this. 

I mean, I've had times where I was sad, sure. Like when my dad passed away, that was hard. Really hard. I missed work for a few days, and I definitely cried then. But even then, even with that kind of grief, I still got up. I still made sure the gutters were cleaned out, I still made sure my wife's car had oil. I was sad, but I wasn't... paralyzed. I didn't have these voices telling me I was worthless, and I didn't feel this heavy, crushing weight on my chest that wouldn't let me breathe. 

So, no, I've never had an episode like this before. This whole thing, it's just completely foreign to me. I keep turning it over and over in my head, trying to find a reason, trying to find some kind of precedent for it in my past, but there's just nothing there. It's like I'm a completely different person now, and I just don't understand it at all.
Have you ever had an episode of depression before this one that started four months ago?

Doc, I... I feel like we're just spinning our wheels here. I know you've got your checklist, but like I told you just a minute ago, and the minute before that... no. Never. I feel like a broken record, but the answer hasn't changed. 

I mean, I can walk you through every single decade of my life if that helps? Because I've been sitting in that recliner for four months doing nothing but replaying my whole life, trying to figure this out. In my twenties, I was working full-time, taking a few classes at the community college at night. I was exhausted, sure, burning the candle at both ends, living off cheap coffee and whatever my wife could throw in a slow cooker before her shift. But I was happy. I was driven. I was building something. 

Then in my thirties, we had the kids, and suddenly money was really tight, and that mortgage felt like a monster... but I never just gave up. I never sat in a dark room and let the world pass me by while my own brain told me I was a worthless burden. I just worked harder. And my forties? Same thing. Steady. Reliable. The guy who mows the lawn on Saturdays and fixes the leaky sink. 

So, I don't know what you're looking for, or if you think I'm hiding some secret breakdown from 1998, but I'm really not. I swear to you. This... this absolute nightmare, this dead weight that hit me four months ago and these awful things I'm hearing... it is the first time. The only time. I have never been like this before in my entire fifty-four years on this earth. I just... I don't know why I snapped now, I really don't, but this is the first time I've ever fallen into a hole like this.
Is this the first time in your life you've experienced an episode of depression like this, or have you had similar episodes before?

Doc, I... I really don't know how many different ways I can say this. I feel like you're not hearing me, or maybe I'm just not explaining it right, but... yes. Yes, this is the very first time. The only time. I've never had anything even remotely close to this before four months ago. 

I keep telling you, I've lived 54 years as a perfectly normal, functioning person. I don't know why you keep asking me the exact same thing. It's like you think I'm lying, or like there's some kind of rule that says a guy my age can't just suddenly fall apart out of nowhere. But I did. That's exactly what happened. I didn't have some secret depression in my twenties that I forgot about. I didn't hide away in my bedroom for months at a time when I was forty. I was just... me. 

I mean, I've spent literally hundreds of hours since this started just sitting in my house, staring at the wall, going over every single year of my life, trying to find the missing puzzle piece. I've thought about every stressful thing that ever happened to me—when my wife had her surgery, when the basement flooded and ruined all our old photos, when I got passed over for that promotion back in '04. I was upset during all those things. I was stressed. I was human. But I never lost my mind. I never heard things that weren't there. I never felt like my body was made of lead and that the whole world would be better off if I just disappeared. 

So, yes. This is the first time. I don't know what else to tell you. I don't have any past episodes to talk about because they don't exist. This nightmare is completely brand new to me, and I just... I really need you to believe me so we can move past this and figure out how to fix it, because I can't keep answering the same question over and over while my head is screaming at me.
Have you ever had an episode of depression that was successfully treated and went away before this current episode started four months ago?

Doctor, I... I don't know what to do here. I really don't. We keep going in this exact same circle, and it's starting to make me feel like I'm losing my mind even more than I already have. You're asking me if I had a depression that was treated and went away, and I... I don't know how to make it any clearer. No. Never. There was nothing to treat before four months ago because there was nothing wrong with me before four months ago.

I've never taken a pill for my mood in my life. I've never sat in a chair like this and talked to someone like you before. I've never had a therapist, I've never gone to a support group, I've never even read a self-help book. My wife, she reads those books sometimes, the ones about finding your joy or whatever, but I never needed them. I was fine. I was just a regular guy living a regular life. 

I feel like you're digging for a history that just isn't there. And I get it, I do, you're a doctor, you want to find the pattern. But there is no pattern. That's what's so terrifying about this whole thing. If I had been through this before, maybe I wouldn't be so scared right now. Maybe I'd be able to tell myself, "Okay, you beat this in 2012, you can beat it again." But I don't have that. I don't have a success story to look back on because I've never been in the trenches before. 

I've never had to fight my own brain just to get out of bed. I've never had these voices, these awful, cruel voices telling me I'm a burden, telling me my family would be better off if I just wasn't here anymore. That's all new. Every single agonizing second of the last four months is completely unprecedented in my life. So, no, I haven't had a treated episode. I haven't had an untreated episode. I haven't had any episodes. Just this one. Just this massive, heavy, suffocating thing that dropped on me out of nowhere. Please, Doc, you have to believe me. We have to move on from this question, because I just don't have a different answer to give you.
Have you ever had any periods where your depressive symptoms completely went away for at least two months before returning?

Doc... I... I honestly think I'm being pranked right now. Are you... are you just reading from a list of questions and you have to get through every single bullet point no matter what I say? Because I feel like I'm screaming into a void here. 

You're asking if the symptoms went away for two months? How... how could they have gone away for two months and returned if the whole thing only started four months ago and hasn't stopped for a single second? It hasn't gone away for two minutes, Doctor, let alone two months! 

From the day this dark cloud rolled in, it has been sitting right on my chest, crushing me. Every single morning, I wake up, and before I even open my eyes, the weight is already there. It's like I'm pinned to the mattress. And those voices I told you about... they don't take a vacation. They don't give me a two-month break to catch my breath or pretend I'm a normal guy again. They are just there, constantly, every single day, telling me how useless I am, how I'm just draining my family. They don't stop. None of this stops. 

So, no. No, it hasn't completely gone away. It hasn't partially gone away. There was no period where it left and came back, because it never left. I really don't understand what we're doing here. I'm sitting here telling you my brain is torturing me, that I'm trapped in this relentless, unbroken hell, and you're asking me about some imaginary gap in the middle of it. 

Please, I am begging you, look at me. Listen to the words coming out of my mouth. Four months. One continuous nightmare. Never stopped. Never went away. Can we please, please talk about how to make it stop now instead of looking for some break in the timeline that just flat out does not exist?
Have you ever had an episode of depression before this current one that started four months ago?

I... I actually don't know what to say anymore. I am completely baffled. Did you... did you not hear me just a second ago? Or the time before that? Or the time before that? 

No. The answer is still no. I have never, not once, not in my entire fifty-four years on this earth, had an episode before this one. 

I don't know if your computer is glitching or if you just have a rigid little checklist that you're forced to read from top to bottom, but it's like my words are just evaporating the second they leave my mouth. I've been sitting here pouring my heart out, telling you how I lived a completely normal life. I went to college, I got married, I worked, I did all the mundane things a regular guy does, and I never, ever had this happen. Not when I was twenty, not when I was thirty, not when I was forty. 

It wasn't until exactly four months ago that the bottom just completely fell out of my world. Before that? Nothing. No episodes. No hidden darkness. Just a regular life. I don't have any past history of this to give you, no matter how many different ways you phrase the question. None. Zero. 

Can we please, please move on to something else now? Because this loop we are stuck in is honestly making my head pound, and I just... I need you to actually listen to the words I am saying so we can focus on what's happening to me right now instead of looking for something in my past that doesn't exist.
Have you ever had any other episodes of depression in your life before the current one?

Are you... I mean, are you serious right now? I'm sorry, I'm just... I'm stunned. I am completely and utterly stunned. 

We literally just went over this. We went over this three times. I feel like I'm in some kind of twisted psychology experiment where they put a guy in a room and ask him the exact same question fifty times just to see when he finally snaps. 

No! The answer is still no! I have never had any other episodes of depression in my life before this current one. I don't know how to make this any clearer. I really don't. I'm a fifty-four-year-old man. For fifty-three years and eight months, my brain worked fine. I woke up, I made my coffee, I read the paper, I went about my day, and I never felt this crushing weight. I never heard voices telling me I'm worthless. I never felt like I was drowning in my own head. 

I've told you about my life. I told you about how I was just a regular guy. I've given you every detail of how this all started four months ago. And yet, here we are, circling back to the exact same question like none of that ever happened. 

Is there a manager here? Or a supervisor? Because I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall. I am desperate for help. I am drowning, Doctor. I am drowning, and instead of throwing me a life preserver, you're asking me if I've ever drowned before! What does it matter?! Even if I had—which I haven't, I swear to God I haven't—what difference would it make right now? 

I need you to stop reading from that damn script and look at me. Look at the man sitting in front of you who is begging for help. Please, I am asking you, man to man, can we talk about what is happening to me right now? Can we talk about how to stop the voices? Can we talk about how to lift this weight? Because if you ask me one more time if I've been depressed before four months ago, I think I'm going to lose whatever tiny shred of sanity I have left.

Even... even just grilling for the family. We used to do burgers and dogs every Sunday afternoon if the weather was decent. The kids would come over, maybe some neighbors. I loved being the guy at the grill, flipping burgers, handing out beers. Now, my wife suggests it and I just feel this pit in my stomach. It's just... it's a terrifying place to be in your own head.
